package_info.package_versions: All versions prior to 5.3.18 and 5.2.20 (Java 9+ required)
package_info.why_malicious: The vulnerability (CVE-2022-22965, 'SpringShell') allows remote attackers to exploit Spring Web's data binding mechanism to manipulate internal ClassLoader and Tomcat attributes via crafted HTTP POST requests. This enables arbitrary file write and remote code execution (RCE) on affected Spring Web applications running on Java 9+ and Tomcat, allowing attackers to deploy web shells and execute arbitrary commands.

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when a crafted HTTP POST request is sent to a Spring Web endpoint that accepts POJOs and binds request parameters to Java objects.
execution_context.file_location: Any exposed Spring Web controller endpoint that performs data binding on user-supplied input.
required_permissions: network (to send HTTP requests to the application)
filesystem (to allow Tomcat to write files to the web root directory)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the attacker sends a crafted HTTP POST request to a vulnerable Spring Web endpoint, which leverages data binding to manipulate Tomcat's internal logging configuration, causing Tomcat to write a new .jsp file containing attacker-controlled code to a web-accessible directory, resulting in the creation of a web shell.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: This behavior allows external, untrusted input to reconfigure Tomcat's internal logging pipeline and write arbitrary files to the web root, which is a clear violation of application security boundaries and enables code execution.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Normal Spring Web applications should never allow user-supplied POST parameters to alter ClassLoader or Tomcat context attributes, nor should they permit arbitrary file creation in web-accessible directories via HTTP requests.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: Legitimate configuration of Tomcat logging and file creation is performed by administrators through secure configuration files or management interfaces, never via user HTTP requests or data binding.
key_indicators: HTTP POST parameters with names starting with class.module.classLoader.*
Modification of Tomcat pipeline attributes (e.g., directory, suffix, prefix, pattern) via HTTP input
Creation of .jsp files in webapps/ROOT or other web-accessible directories
pattern parameter containing web shell or executable code payload

execution_context.trigger: At runtime, when an HTTP GET request is made to the newly created malicious .jsp file after it has been written to the web root.
execution_context.file_location: webapps/ROOT/ohno.jsp (or another attacker-chosen path within a web-accessible directory)
required_permissions: network (to access the web shell via HTTP GET)
filesystem (to execute the .jsp file written to disk)

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, after the malicious JSP file is created, the attacker sends an HTTP GET request to the new .jsp file, which executes the embedded web shell code, allowing the attacker to execute arbitrary system commands on the server and gain remote code execution.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Execution of attacker-controlled code via a newly created, web-accessible JSP file is a classic remote code execution pattern and indicates a successful exploitation of the application.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Web applications should not allow arbitrary file creation or execution of user-supplied code. Only trusted, pre-deployed JSP files should be present and executable in the web root.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: JSP files are used for dynamic web content, but should only be deployed and managed by trusted developers or administrators, not created dynamically via user input.
key_indicators: Unexpected .jsp files appearing in web root or webapps/ROOT directory
JSP code containing command execution logic (e.g., Runtime.getRuntime().exec)
Immediate access to new .jsp file following suspicious POST request

attack_chain.action: Attacker identifies a POST endpoint in the Spring application that accepts POJOs and performs data binding on user input.
attack_chain.leads_to: Ability to send crafted POST requests to manipulate internal server attributes via data binding.

attack_chain.action: Attacker sends a crafted HTTP POST request with class.module.classLoader.* parameters to reconfigure Tomcat's logging pipeline, specifying a .jsp file with attacker-controlled content.
attack_chain.leads_to: Arbitrary file write of a malicious JSP web shell to a web-accessible directory.

attack_chain.action: Attacker triggers a logging event (or relies on normal application logging) to ensure the malicious code is written to the new .jsp file.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malicious JSP file is now present on the server in the web root.

attack_chain.action: Attacker accesses the new .jsp file via HTTP GET, causing the server to execute the embedded web shell code.
attack_chain.leads_to: Remote code execution on the server, allowing the attacker to run arbitrary commands.

behavioral_signatures: HTTP POST requests with parameters prefixed by class.module.classLoader.* targeting Spring Web endpoints
Unexpected changes to Tomcat logging configuration at runtime via HTTP input
Creation of new .jsp files in web-accessible directories (e.g., webapps/ROOT)
Execution of newly created .jsp files containing web shell or command execution code
file_indicators: webapps/ROOT/ohno.jsp (or other unexpected .jsp files in web root or webapps/ROOT)
JSP files containing suspicious code patterns such as Runtime.getRuntime().exec or similar command execution logic
network_indicators: Unusual HTTP POST requests to Spring endpoints with class.module.classLoader.* parameters
Subsequent HTTP GET requests to newly created .jsp files in the web root
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for HTTP POST requests containing class.module.classLoader.* parameters, especially those targeting Spring Web endpoints that perform data binding. Alert on the creation of new .jsp files in web-accessible directories and on execution of JSP files not present in the original deployment. Review Tomcat configuration changes at runtime and scan for JSP files containing suspicious code patterns such as command execution logic (e.g., Runtime.getRuntime().exec). Correlate suspicious POST requests with subsequent access to new .jsp files to identify exploitation attempts.
